$data.description: Reusable contracts for observed Command Hub facts supplied by the host rather than authored into a version.

lf-worktree.description: Current worktree evidence keyed by the id of its authored lf-worktree seat.

guidance.coordinator:
After worktree evidence changes, replace the complete page-bound source snapshot rather than republishing it as prose or appending an event:

```bash
leaf data set "$PAGE" <source-id> --file worktrees.json
```

Read `data_bindings` from `leaf page state "$PAGE"` to find source ids using the `lf-worktree` contract and their consuming widget ids. `worktrees.json` is an object keyed by authored worktree widget id. Each value carries `branch`, `base`, `head`, non-negative `ahead`, `behind`, `additions`, `deletions`, and `commits`, a `tests` value of `passing`, `failing`, `running`, or `not-run`, an RFC 3339 `observedAt` timestamp with a timezone, and optional `files` and `diff` strings. Keep a key stable for the same worktree. Gather these facts with host tools; Leaf validates, transports, and presents them but does not run git or inspect worker directories.

$command.description: The optional Command Hub projection. Each widget names the general role it plays and the attributes that carry that role's state. Later packages may add their own tag entries under widgets without teaching Leaf's kernel their names.

lf-roster.description:
Who is working, and where each of them stands right now. Children are lf-agent elements only. Where lf-tasks is the work and lf-milestones the schedule, a roster is the other axis a page running several workers needs: the tree says a task is active, and only the roster says which of five sessions is holding it, what that one is doing this minute, and whether anybody has heard from it since breakfast. Reach for it on a page one orchestrator publishes and several workers report to — the standing hub arrangement — and leave it off a page with one agent on it, where the banner already says everything a roster would.

It stands wider than the prose column where the window has the room (x-wide), because a roster is read across rather than down: the comparison a reader wants is one agent's line against the next, and a column narrow enough for prose puts each line's own facts on two rows and destroys it.
lf-roster.x-example: wren Holds the feeder rebuild end to end. finch Baffles are fitted and green; the work is yours to read. junco Free — nothing assigned since the corpus snapshot.

lf-agent.description:
One worker: a session, an agent, a person. Lead with a <strong> name — the identity it reports under — and prose saying its durable remit. On a command surface, placement gives that remit: directly under lf-command means the whole project; directly under an lf-task means that goal and its descendants. This admits coordinators, area owners, and leaf specialists without closing them into a role enum.

The version carries `state` and optional `on`. `state` says where the worker stands: working, waiting, blocked, idle, reaped, or done. `on` is only the current focus and, inside a command, must remain within the structural remit; a broad coordinator or idle worker need not invent one. A report adds the finer-grained `doing` clause and moves the row live until a version absorbs or overrules it. One report verb carries state and doing together so an activity sentence cannot split across fold coordinates; only state creates record debt because a version can adjudicate an enum but not a clause that was true for one minute. Branch and worktree evidence belong to a page-bound external source rather than to authored worker prose.

The row computes when the log last heard from this worker, even past an absorbed report. A working claim silent for the shared quarter-hour grace is called out, so the banner and fleet mean the same thing by quiet. The row remains a view; a nested decision carries any work for the reader.

lf-tasks.description: A hierarchy of work: what a project is made of, who holds each piece, and where each piece stands. Children are lf-task elements, nesting freely — the tree is the plan's own shape, so write the decomposition as it is rather than flattening it. Where lf-milestones is a flat rail of stages on a schedule and lf-board is a set the reviewer re-orders, lf-tasks is structure: a parent's children are what doing it means, and the upgrade counts each parent's subtree into a generated done-fraction chip so the tree reads as progress without a widget of its own. Statuses change through live source revisions, or between saves by a worker's `leaf report` (x-report on lf-task) — the page keeps up with the work — and comments anchor per task, so keep every task's id stable across revisions.
lf-tasks.x-example:
Rebuild the feeders Two of four mounted. Replace the mounts Fit squirrel baffles Ready for review.

Are the baffles ready?

Approve Request changes Heat the bird bath Waiting on a transformer delivery.

lf-command.description: A goal-first command surface. Its nested goals are the one authored plan; each worker lives once at the narrowest tree level matching its durable remit — directly under the command for project-wide coordination, or under any goal for that goal's whole subtree. `on` is only the worker's current focus inside that remit. The orchestration upgrade derives the operator header, stopped-work reading, and live-worker projection from this tree. `label` and `phase` name the outcome and planning horizon. Do not author a second roster or decisions list beside it: those are views of the tree and its log. Later packages may add their own goal or worker widgets under `$command.widgets` without teaching Leaf's kernel their names.
lf-command.x-example: lead Coordinates the whole garden. Rebuild the feeders w-1 Fitting the baffles.

lf-task.description: One piece of the work. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows, and child lf-task elements after the prose are its decomposition. `status` colors the marker: planned, active, blocked (stuck — the prose says on what), review (finished by whoever held it and ready to be reviewed), stalled (work produced no durable progress), or done. Status describes the work. Reader work is a nested Decision whose widget supplies the answer control; the task rolls that decision through the plan but never originates one. `owner` names who holds the work, `when` is a free-text schedule label, and `tags` adds one chip per entry. A parent with children gets a generated done-fraction chip. The `status` report is provisional agent state (`leaf report <page> <task-id> status status=review`); a stamped version absorbs or overrules it through `overruled` (see $report).

lf-worktree.description: One stable address for a disposable worker's inspectable evidence. Author an empty element with an id and bind its `worktrees` input through the `source` attribute. The widget projects the matching record into the element and keeps datum comments attached when a later snapshot replaces it. Branch, divergence, diffstat, test result, file tree, and diff are observed data rather than authored version state.

x-guidance.author:
Keep one empty, stable worktree address beside each worker whose evidence the host can inspect:

```html
<lf-worktree id="tree-wren" source="project-worktrees"></lf-worktree>
```

The page chooses the source id. Reuse one id for widgets that read the same snapshot, or use different ids when a page has independent worktree feeds. Do not author branch, diffstat, tests, file tree, or diff into the version; the host supplies those observed facts through the bound source, and comments stay attached by worktree and datum keys when the snapshot changes.

lf-worktree.x-example: wren Owns the feed rebuild.

lf-operations.description: A set of consequential host operations offered for one goal and its exact disposable worker and worktree. Put a live set inside lf-decision, whose leading heading states the question; each lf-operation child supplies the reader-facing argument while this holder sends one typed x-request carrying those three stable ids. The ready holder is one of the reader's decisions; an accepted request hands the turn to the host and locks the set while it works. `leaf receipt` links one succeeded or failed outcome. Failure returns the decision and reopens the controls, while success leaves the completed instruction visible until a later authored revision updates the plan. Use this for effects such as starting a worker, landing a branch, or archiving work. Use lf-options instead for a policy or authored-state decision that Leaf itself can replay.

x-guidance.author: Use `<lf-operations>` when pressing a choice should ask the host to do something irreversible or externally observable. Set `target`, `worker`, and `worktree` to the stable page ids for the goal and exact disposable host objects the operation acts on, then place one `<lf-operation verb="…">` per offered command inside it. The package owns the allowed verbs; do not encode a command in an lf-option id or prose and ask the coordinator to guess it.
x-guidance.coordinator:
A `request` event from this widget is an instruction to act, not replayable page state. Dispatch on its declared `action` and typed `detail.target`, `detail.worker`, and `detail.worktree`; verify those exact objects and current host state, and use the request id as the operation's idempotency and reconciliation key. On first delivery, perform the operation once using the host's native task/worktree tools. When recovering a pending request after interruption, inspect the host for that key and the requested result before acting; resume or record the existing outcome instead of starting, merging, or removing twice. Then always append the one terminal outcome:

```bash
leaf receipt "$PAGE" <request-id> succeeded --text "Started w-9 on the preserved branch"
# or
leaf receipt "$PAGE" <request-id> failed --text "Branch no longer exists"
```

Never acknowledge the wait batch until the request has reached the durable executor that owns the host task handle. `restart` preserves the named worktree, reaps the named worker, and launches a fresh worker for `target`; `park` removes the target from the active plan without discarding the named worktree; `drop` reaps the named worker and archives its worktree; `land` merges the named worktree; `hold` keeps it unmerged; `request-changes` retains the review request and starts a fresh revision worker from that worktree; `land-as-is` lands the named worktree and retires the named reviser. After success, refresh bound external data and save the plan revision the operation produced; stamp it when the result is a useful checkpoint. Leaf validates and records this protocol but does not call host APIs itself.

lf-operations.x-example:
Review the branch review-worker Owns the reviewed branch.

What should the host do?

Land it Tests are green. My take: land while the evidence is current. Request changes Start a fresh reviser.

lf-operation.description: One reader-facing command inside lf-operations. `verb` chooses a request declaration on the holder; the child prose explains the consequence and remains selectable. State the author's preference as ordinary prose in the operation itself, such as `My take: land while the evidence is current.`. The holder owns the gesture and the target so sibling commands are one atomic choice surface.

lf-record.description: The page's consequential action receipts, projected in log order. It renders reader actions, external requests and their linked receipts, held comments, resolutions, reports, and publications with their targets and payload summaries. Folds and read-only disclosures do not enter because the log never recorded them. This is evidence, not another state store.
